name: The heron people
land: A low shore where a slow river meets still water. Reed beds, a jetty, houses on stilts, and one post standing at the water's edge with a heron cut into it.

myths.title: The woman and the heron
myths.text: Before there were people at the water's edge there was only the water, and in it the heron, standing. A woman came down from the dry country with nothing in her hands. She was hungry, and she asked the heron for a fish. The heron gave her one. She asked again the next day, and the heron gave her another, and asked for nothing. On the third day she was ashamed. She had taken twice and given nothing, and she had nothing to give. So she pulled reeds and knotted them, one knot for each fish she had eaten, and went on knotting until she had made the first net. With the net she caught more than she needed. She carried the first fish to the heron and laid it down, and only then did she eat. The heron ate, and stayed. Others came down from the dry country after her. She showed each of them the knot, and told each of them the same thing: the heron eats first. Those who learned the knot stayed, and they are the people. Those who would not learn it went back up to the dry country, and nothing more is told of them.

myths.title: The year the fish went down
myths.text: There was a man called Ket who was better with a net than anyone living. One evening his catch was so large that the first fish out of it was a small one, and he thought it a poor thing to carry to the post. He ate it himself and meant to bring a better one in the morning. In the morning the nets came up empty. They came up empty the next day, and for all that season. The fish had gone down to where the water is dark, and the heron was not seen at the post. Children grew thin. Ket's mother, who was the eldest then, did not ask him what he had done; everyone knew. She walked into the water at dusk and stood there as the heron stands, through the night and the next day, without eating and without speaking. At the second dusk the heron came back and stood beside her. The fish came up. Ket lived a long time after that, but he never again ate before the eldest of his house had eaten, and when he mended a net he left one knot untied. People still leave it.

myths.title: The knot that is owed
myths.text: When a child of the people is born, the eldest of the house ties a knot in the house net and says the child's name into it. That knot is the child's debt: everything the child will eat before it can fish was caught by someone else. A child cannot pay it. When the child is grown and brings home a first catch, nothing is untied. Instead the grown child ties a second knot beside the first, for someone not yet born. So no one of the people ever pays what they owe to those who fed them. They pay it to those who come after, and the net grows longer. When someone dies, the house net is carried to the water at dusk, and the dead one's first knot is cut out and given to the water, going downstream. The rest of the net stays with the living. It is said that a net with no knots cut from it is a net that has caught nothing, and that a house which keeps its dead knots will find its nets empty. No one says who first said this.

entries.statement: The heron stands for the dead, who gave to the living before they were asked.
A knot stands for a debt: something received that must be answered.
What you were given cannot be paid back to the giver; it is paid forward to those who come after.

entries.topic: the two directions of the water
entries.statement: Upstream belongs to the living and to beginnings; downstream belongs to the dead and to endings.
Dusk is the hour when the dead are near, which is why what is owed to them is given then.
To be given to is to be bound, and to take without answering is the deepest shame.
The untied knot in every net is the people's memory of Ket's fault: no one's giving is ever complete.
The dry country stands for a life without debt, which the people regard as no life at all.
The first fish of every catch is carried to the post and left for the heron before anyone eats.

entries.topic: a thing people say at meals
entries.statement: The people say: the heron eats first, we eat after.

entries.topic: how the first fish is carried
entries.statement: No one speaks while the first fish is carried to the post, and the carrier walks back without turning round.
Every net has one knot left untied.

entries.topic: what is done at a birth
entries.statement: At a birth the eldest of the house ties a knot in the house net and says the child's name into it.

entries.topic: what is done at a first catch
entries.statement: When a grown child brings home a first catch, they tie a second knot beside their birth knot.

entries.topic: the order of eating in a house
entries.statement: No one eats before the eldest of their house has eaten.
The people came down from the dry country, which lies above the water's edge.
Ket was the best net-man of his time and is remembered for eating a first fish himself.
In the year the fish went down, the nets came up empty for a whole season.
The people say: a net with no knots cut from it has caught nothing.
The post with the heron cut into it stands where the first fish was first laid down.
A guest is fed before the house eats, but after the heron.
It is shameful to refuse food that is offered.
The net-menders mend every house's net and keep the count of its knots.
Whoever takes fish from another house's net owes that house a day's mending.

entries.topic: what is done at a death
entries.statement: When someone dies, the house net is carried to the water at dusk and their birth knot is cut out and given to the water, downstream.

entries.topic: what the eldest owes in a bad season
entries.statement: In an empty season the eldest must stand in the water from dusk to dusk without eating or speaking.
A house must never keep the knots of its dead.
Ket's mother stood in the water and brought the fish back, and her name is not spoken.
The name said into a birth knot is not said aloud again until the child's first catch; until then the child is called by a water-name.
Those who went back to the dry country are not hated; they are pitied, and they are not spoken of.

customs.name: Feeding the heron
customs.visible: At dusk, whoever has fished carries one fish to the post in silence, lays it at the foot, and walks back without turning round.

customs.name: The open knot
customs.visible: When a net is finished or mended, the last knot is left loose and hangs open.

customs.name: The birth knot
customs.visible: After a birth, the oldest person of the house ties a knot into a long net that hangs indoors, and whispers into it.

customs.name: Feeding the guest
customs.visible: A visitor is given food as soon as they sit, before anyone of the house touches theirs, and people watch until the visitor has eaten.

customs.name: Giving the knot to the water
customs.visible: At dusk a house carries a long net to the water; one small piece is cut from it and let go on the current.

villagers.name: Maëlle
villagers.temperament: dry, patient, exact about small things
villagers.slant: She tells the stories as stories about work done properly: knots tied right, counts kept. She has no patience for anyone who makes the heron into something to be afraid of.

lines.refusal: That is for the shaman to say. I mend nets.
lines.withholding: That is not for a stranger.

villagers.name: Old Tam
villagers.temperament: gruff, fond of being right, kinder than he sounds
villagers.slant: He was a boy the last time the nets came up empty for a month. Nobody stood in the water that time, and the fish came back anyway. He thinks the fish went down in Ket's year because the water turned cold, and that the story was fitted to it afterwards. He still carries his first fish to the post. He says a man can doubt a story and keep a habit.

lines.withholding: You have not been here long enough for that.
lines.redirect: {name} would know. Go and bother them.

villagers.name: Ysolt
villagers.temperament: ceremonious, slow to speak, hard to hurry
villagers.slant: She tells each story the same way every time and dislikes questions in the middle. She believes an empty season could come again, and that it would be hers to answer.

lines.refusal: That is the shaman's to say, and I will not say it in the shaman's place.
lines.withholding: That is not said to a guest.

villagers.name: Minnow

knowsMyths.version: A hungry woman asked the heron for a fish and the heron gave her one, and then another. She was sorry she had nothing to give back, so she made a net and gave the heron the first fish. That is why the heron eats first.
A man ate the first fish himself, and all the fish went away for a long time. Then they came back. So nobody does that.

villagers.slant: Minnow finds carrying the first fish boring and the silence hard, and wonders out loud whether the heron is ever full. Minnow repeats what grown-ups say without always knowing why.

lines.refusal: I don't know. You'd have to ask the shaman.

villagers.name: Corin
villagers.temperament: restless, proud of his first catch, quick to take offence
villagers.slant: He thinks about the dry country more than he lets on, and wonders what the ones who went back found there. He tells the first story with more interest in those who left than in those who stayed.

lines.refusal: Nobody ever told me that. The shaman would know.
lines.redirect: {name} knows that better than I do.

villagers.name: Besa
villagers.slant: She tells the first story as a story about shame: the woman's shame at eating twice and giving nothing. She presses food on a visitor and takes a refusal personally.

lines.refusal: Ah, that one is for the shaman.
lines.withholding: That is not for a guest's ears, forgive me.
lines.redirect: Go and ask {name}, and then come back and eat.
